knowledge.question: What should I think about before setting up a new Rewards Club season?
knowledge.answer: Plan for what your business will look like over the next 90 days, because you can't change it mid-season. Consider your average sale price, your price range, and whether you'll be bringing in new product. Levi says the most important tier right now is bronze, since getting people in is what turns on the notifications.

knowledge.question: Besides rewards, how else can I bring viewers back?
knowledge.answer: Build a community people want to come back to every day just to say hello. Levi says people click on your notification because they love your live, want to say hi, or find you entertaining, not only to buy. He hops on stream a couple hours a week himself to say hello to his community.

knowledge.question: How did Levi end up selling on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: In early 2025 Levi had about $100,000 of used liquidation inventory he had planned to sell on eBay, but eBay shut down his accounts. On April 26, 2025 he woke up at 5 a.m., asked ChatGPT how to sell $100K of used inventory as fast as possible without eBay, and it said Whatnot. He opened an account that day and went live that afternoon with a goal of just $300 a day to move the inventory. He did $3,000 on his first live and about $8,000 across April 26-28 without knowing what he was doing.

knowledge.question: Why does Levi prefer Whatnot over Amazon FBA?
knowledge.answer: On Amazon his margins were around 10-15% and account health is a big risk: he has seen sellers doing $80 million a year get shut down for two weeks or even three months, which is a disaster when you have employees. On Whatnot he scaled to about $200,000 a month at roughly 45% net profit. He also says Whatnot is very beginner-friendly and lenient on violations and suspensions compared to Amazon.

knowledge.question: How fast do you get your money back on Whatnot compared to Amazon?
knowledge.answer: Levi breaks down Amazon FBA: ordering takes 7-10 days, prep 1-3 days, check-in about two more weeks, then you wait for the stock to sell and another two weeks for payouts, so it's around 60-90 days to get your money back. On Whatnot you can buy from a local supplier, sell it today, and with instant payouts get paid today; even with standard payouts it's about 4 hours after delivery. That much faster cash cycle means lower risk because most of your money is back in your bank at the end of the day.

knowledge.question: Should I leave my balance sitting in my Whatnot account?
knowledge.answer: Levi always zeroes out his Whatnot balance. With instant payouts there are no account reserves on Whatnot, unlike Amazon, which can hold $100K in reserves for two weeks. He says his habit comes from hearing Amazon horror stories, and he recommends always cashing out. TikTok also has reserves, but it's not as bad when you have a rep.

knowledge.question: How quickly should I hire people once my Whatnot shows start working?
knowledge.answer: Levi started on Whatnot April 26, 2025 and was already interviewing streamers while at a seller conference in Miami days later. He had two shippers ready when he got back and hired four stream hosts on May 4. One of them, Kristin, is still with him and built about 75% of the account. Within 12 months his team had sold close to $2 million across multiple accounts.

knowledge.question: What was Levi's first reselling experience before live selling?
knowledge.answer: In 2020 he started selling things from his basement on Facebook Marketplace, Letgo and OfferUp. Then he and his dad split a $1,000 storage unit on storagetreasures.com 50/50 and doubled their money. They focused on units with appliances: if the fridge, stove and washer alone would pay back the unit, everything else was profit. That grew into restaurant equipment, including a deal on four mixers for $8,000 where one sold for $28,000.

knowledge.question: Is losing money on inventory the end of a business?
knowledge.answer: Levi says the $100,000 of eBay liquidation inventory ended up being a loss of about $100K in 2025 after labor and storage, even though he sold a lot of it on Whatnot. But he calls it a blessing in disguise: it's what pushed him onto Whatnot, where he made the money back and much more and has helped many other people do the same. He also says he doesn't like firing people and would rather find a solution, so he kept paying his employee and figured out a way forward.

knowledge.question: Is low-ticket selling worth it if I don't have much capital?
knowledge.answer: Levi says yes. People bash low ticket as not worth their time, but if you're limited on capital it can still reach big numbers. In his example, a seller going at that rate for 30 days straight would be doing about half a million dollars a month and most likely around $150K net profit, and that was from only 7 hours of streaming. Streaming 10 hours a day at that pace, they're killing it.

knowledge.question: Do I need a big personality to sell on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says no. You don't need to pay six figures for a top streamer; as long as you have energy, want to work, and can engage and talk with people, you are a good fit for Whatnot. He does say being introverted is a drawback, because the job is talking to people. Everyone has a story to tell.

knowledge.question: How do I start conversations with viewers during a live show?
knowledge.answer: Levi's two best ways are storytelling and asking questions. Tell stories about what you did yesterday, or what your friend, mom, dad or dog did. Ask questions like 'Is anyone working today?', 'What state are you from?' or 'Who's your favorite artist?'. Those questions often connect two viewers from the same state or with the same taste in music, and then they start talking to each other in the chat.

knowledge.question: Why do sellers ask viewers to comment 'W' in the chat?
knowledge.answer: Levi says it drives engagement in the chat, and engagement feeds the Whatnot algorithm, which pushes more viewers to your show. More viewers means a higher chance of more bids, higher prices, and more people interested in the product. Examples are 'Comment W if you want me to pull the giveaway' or 'Comment W if you want a banger.'

knowledge.question: Is it bad to talk too much instead of selling on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says there are people who want to hear your story and talk to you, not just shop, so don't worry about complaints on Reddit or Facebook groups. You do need a balance, because you still have to sell and make money. His viewers tell him they like his shows because he teaches them and engages the most.

knowledge.question: How long does it take a new streamer to get good?
knowledge.answer: Levi says selling, showing and describing the product while talking to the community is multitasking and takes practice; do it for a couple of months and you'll get the hang of it. His main streamer Kristen started in May 2025 as the worst of his four original streamers, and he almost fired her. By February 2026 she was the best, the only one still with him, and had built about 70% of the account and its relationships herself.

knowledge.question: Do buyers get attached to a specific streamer?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi says some people show up to his streamer Kristen's shows instead of his. When she was away for almost two months, buyers kept asking if she was coming back, and some who didn't show up to other streams started buying again when she returned. He says people buy for the inventory, the streamer, free shipping, or the group of people on the account.

knowledge.question: Can being entertaining on camera actually increase my viewers?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi says you don't only have to sell; you can be funny. When a buyer bought an item and asked him to throw a glass bottle, he did it on camera with the buyer's permission, and the show went up 30 viewers. It's part of the show, it's entertainment.

knowledge.question: How should I handle a bad day on a live show?
knowledge.answer: Levi says don't scream and don't get upset if the day is bad. Every day is different: some days you'll make $100 profit and the next day $5,000. You can even be honest with your community that you're feeling down. Just keep going and be yourself.

knowledge.question: Who is Whatnot best for, and who is TikTok Shop best for?
knowledge.answer: Levi says Whatnot is great for beginners and was life-changing for him. TikTok Shop is game-changing for big businesses that want to do millions of dollars a month. TikTok will reach out to help you and wants you to hit eight figures, while Whatnot never reached out to him or offered help.

knowledge.question: How do I expand from Whatnot to TikTok Shop live auctions?
knowledge.answer: Replicate the system you already built on Whatnot. Levi says the two platforms have very similar systems and back-end teams, so all he had to do was copy what he had on Whatnot over to TikTok and double down. Because they had the cash for it, they went from four or five streamers to 12 streamers a day.

knowledge.question: What happens if I get TikTok Shop violations on my live auctions?
knowledge.answer: Levi says violations are a huge thing on TikTok, nearly one every day for random reasons. On their first day they got a violation for selling too low, even though it's an auction: with about a $12 average, some prices will go low, but they're profitable because they buy between $1 and $3, or under $1 for things like keychains. If you don't have a rep to clear those violations, TikTok can limit your account, your payouts and your daily orders. Levi and his brother have reps who make commission off their sales, so the reps help them with these AI violations.

knowledge.question: How hard is it to get a TikTok Shop appeal approved or get onto TikTok Live Auction?
knowledge.answer: It's a process. Levi submitted all the documents and the required videos twice, and the AI still didn't approve it. Getting both of his accounts onboarded to TikTok Live Auction took 4 weeks, while his brother's account was fine from day one but still gets violations almost every day. Without a rep to push appeals through, which some of his students struggle with, your account might stay restricted and you could be stuck selling about 10 items a day. That's why he says TikTok Live Auction is not beginner-friendly if you don't have a rep.

knowledge.question: Why does moving fast matter so much on a Whatnot show?
knowledge.answer: People have short attention spans, and Levi's data shows his buyers stay in a show around 45 minutes to an hour, close to Whatnot's figure of about 90 minutes a day on the app. His team sells around two items per minute, so you can see from item numbers and auction timestamps how long someone stayed. If you move slowly, viewers leave before they buy. There are also so many new buyers coming into your store that you can change your setup from one day to the next and half the people in your live wouldn't even notice.

knowledge.question: Should I write lot numbers on my items by hand during random pulls?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi says writing 1, 2, 3 with a pen or marker takes too long and causes human error, and it took his team 3 months to stop doing it. Instead, ask ChatGPT to make a PDF of 2x1 labels numbered from 1 to 2,000, buy cheap 2x1 labels on Amazon, and print them on a thermal printer so you save on ink (his roll printer has lasted 2 years). Print the labels big with a thick font that fills the whole 2x1 label so the numbers are hard to misread.

knowledge.question: How many number labels should I print before a show?
knowledge.answer: Print on demand from your numbered PDF. If you plan 100 items, print pages 1 to 100; if the show is going well, take a 1-minute break and print 100 to 200, then 200 to 300 if you keep going. Levi's team usually prints 1 to 500 for a 6-hour show and 1 to 1,000 when they plan a fast-paced show or want to push harder. On a really good day he recommends running even longer than planned.

knowledge.question: How should I store sold items during a show so shipping is easy?
knowledge.answer: Buy shelves on wheels and line the sold items up in number order like a bookshelf: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. When a shelf fills up, roll it out and bring in another one. At shipping time everything is already in order, so packers can grab 442, 443, 444 straight from the packing slip. The order also catches mistakes, because if a printer skips a number you'll see the gap on the shelf right away. Levi prefers carts and shelves to bins because you can squeeze in more product and you don't have to dig.

knowledge.question: How do I organize really small items like beauty products?
knowledge.answer: For his beauty streams, Levi uses numbered boxes of 10 (1-10, 10-20, and so on) on wheeled shelves instead of lining items up individually. It's much easier to look through a box of 10 than a box of 100. He puts about four boxes on each tier, which fits roughly 200 items per shelf, and his team runs up to 1,000 items in a beauty show because the items are small and the pace is faster.

knowledge.question: What equipment do I need for my selling station?
knowledge.answer: Levi's setup is simple: a table (ideally on wheels), a tripod or ring light with the phone that streams (they use an iPhone 16/17), some good lighting, and a second phone to start auctions. Don't start auctions from a laptop because it takes too many clicks; the app is made for mobile, where you just tap start next. If you don't have a second device, you can start auctions on the streaming phone. Raise the product so it sits above the halfway point on screen, because the chat covers the bottom of the video.

knowledge.question: How should I set up the space around my stream?
knowledge.answer: Don't put your stream in a corner, because you need space to move carts in and out. Levi's flow is: a shelf of unsold product on your left, run the item on the stand, label it, then put it on a cart on your right once it's sold. Empty carts come in from behind and sold carts roll out to the shipping area behind the scenes. In a corner you have to keep pushing shelves in and out, which slows everything down.

knowledge.question: Do I need a helper passing me products while I stream?
knowledge.answer: Only if you have a lot of viewers. Levi says if you're pulling 30 or 40 viewers, customers will wait for you if you have a connection with them, and smaller streams tend to have a more personal relationship with the host. Once you have around 100 viewers and plan to sell 200 to 500 items in a show, a helper makes sense. Even then, you can often just load a shelf on your left before the show and grab from it yourself.

knowledge.question: How long should my auction timer be?
knowledge.answer: It depends on the price and how many people want the item. For $3 to $5 sales you should move as fast as possible, since it's easy to hit $5 in 5 seconds. For higher-ticket items, be careful with a 10-second sudden death because people may need longer to put in a bid, and you lose potential profit if they miss it. Levi suggests a 20-second timer or 10 plus 10 for those items. A 10-second sudden death does create urgency, but only when enough people want the product.

knowledge.question: Why should I stay live for more hours or hire more streamers?
knowledge.answer: In live auctions you're selling a product every 10, 20 or 30 seconds, or at least every minute. Levi says if you're not live, you're not making money. You could be generating profit all day long, and the only reason you aren't is that you didn't hire. He says you can't make sales that constantly on Amazon, eBay or Poshmark, only with live selling on Whatnot and TikTok.

knowledge.question: How do I set profit goals for my live shows?
knowledge.answer: Levi's formula for working toward six figures: start by figuring out how many hours of live you need to produce $500 in profit. Then work out the hours for $1,000 in profit, and keep scaling the target, using your profit per unit to work out how many units you need to sell.

knowledge.question: Should I start live selling on Whatnot or TikTok?
knowledge.answer: Start with Whatnot. Levi has made seven figures on both, and he says Whatnot is still the number one platform to start on. The audience and community there are completely different, buyer intention is much higher, and some buyers don't even like buying on TikTok. Don't get distracted by TikTok looking shiny; just get started on Whatnot, and if you can, get help from someone who has done both.

knowledge.question: How do I attract buyers to my Whatnot show?
knowledge.answer: Levi says it's a mix of the host and the inventory. He highly recommends prepping for every show; one of his students prepped for her first show and did very well.

knowledge.question: How much should I pay my Whatnot hosts?
knowledge.answer: Levi pays hosts hourly, starting at $18 an hour and going up from there with seniority. He used to start at $22 an hour but it didn't make sense to pay a new host the same as someone who'd been with him six months. He doesn't set revenue or items-sold targets per streamer because every day is different.

knowledge.question: I'm new to liquidation. Where should I start sourcing?
knowledge.answer: Start with your local liquidator; there are liquidators everywhere. Your local liquidator likely started with a few pallets, moved up to truckloads because it's cheaper per pallet, and now sells by the pallet. You can find them by searching Facebook Marketplace or Google for things like 'Target pallets for sale' and picking something close so you can go in person.

knowledge.question: What category should I sell in as a streamer?
knowledge.answer: Levi says sell whatever you can source and whatever you're knowledgeable about or would enjoy selling. He personally wouldn't host a health and beauty show because he doesn't know much about it. If he were starting this month, he'd suggest toys, which are doing very well.

knowledge.question: How do I avoid getting scammed when buying pallets?
knowledge.answer: Do test buys and go in person. Touch the physical product, look at it, and put your hand at the bottom of the pallet to make sure it isn't padded with pillows. Levi got scammed $3,000 on pallets in 2021, and says shaking hands and meeting people is how you succeed in this business.

knowledge.question: Are Target pallets better than Amazon pallets?
knowledge.answer: Right now Levi only buys Target because the supply has been very new or new open box, so the quality is higher and it takes less labor than Amazon returns. Amazon goods still work, but you have to inspect them very thoroughly. He prefers manifested loads only.

knowledge.question: What percent of retail should I pay for inventory?
knowledge.answer: Levi says 15% of retail is a solid start, even 20%. The more you sell, the lower that percentage goes; he buys as low as 5% of retail because he buys at higher volume. He would rarely pay over 50% of retail, and the cheaper you buy, the less labor eats into your profit.

knowledge.question: What price per unit should I aim to buy at?
knowledge.answer: Levi's buying criteria is under $2 a piece. That way he can start an item at $1, and if it sells for $4, he still made money before labor.

knowledge.question: Why is it hard to lose money buying liquidation for Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: If you're buying at 10–15% of retail, the general public will happily compete to pay at least 20–30%. For example, if something is valued at $100 and you paid $15 or $20, two people will compete to pay $30 because they know it goes for $100. Levi says Whatnot is the best way to enter the liquidation market for that reason.

knowledge.question: Should I start my auctions at $1?
knowledge.answer: Not necessarily. Levi says you determine what your product is worth; if you think it's worth a dollar, that's what it's worth to you. He regularly starts high-end products at $200, $300 or $500, and says people quit on day one because they think they have to start everything at $1. On a good day he'll start some high-ticket items at $1 just for the dopamine effect, accepting that they might go for around 40% of retail.

knowledge.question: Why do big sellers run 10-second auctions?
knowledge.answer: Speed. Levi says they're essentially wholesaling to the public, and moving fast is what lets them offer those deals. The algorithm also likes speed because Whatnot earns a percentage of every sale, so the faster and more you sell, the more they boost your stream.

knowledge.question: Should I ask chat what they want me to run?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi says the biggest beginner mistake he sees is asking the chat what they want. Just run the product, even if you don't think it'll sell, because someone new is walking into your show every second. He still reminds his hosts to just run it.

knowledge.question: Is it better to run auctions or do random pulls?
knowledge.answer: Levi says the more time you spend sorting products, the more labor it costs. His team doesn't list everything; they pull out only the high-end products for the shelf (since they shouldn't sell those under 50% of retail) and move the rest quickly through bundles and pulls.

knowledge.question: Should my show have 100 different items or 100 of the same item?
knowledge.answer: 100 different items, 100%. Levi says this isn't Amazon FBA where you send 100 units and wait. You want customers to stay on your show for entertainment and be able to buy multiple different products, and he recommends having a minimum of 100 products in a show so buyers can keep filling their bundle.

knowledge.question: Can I run the same products over and over in a show?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi's analytics show about 70% of his buyers each day are new. Over one weekend plus Monday they got about 500 new buyers while running the same five to seven products around 500 times, and it sold well. Returning buyers may get a little upset, but there are new people on the app every day.

knowledge.question: What are your top tips to grow a new stream?
knowledge.answer: Levi's top three: be consistent, be quick with your auctions, and don't ask the chat what they want, just run. One weekend, 12,000 to 20,000 different people per day watched his show for over 30 seconds while it peaked around 200 concurrent viewers, so someone is always entering and leaving. Approach every moment like someone just walked in, and ask 'Who's new here? Who's new to the app?'

knowledge.question: What elevated your Whatnot channel the most?
knowledge.answer: Consistency. Levi says his first month they could barely hold 30 to 50 viewers, and growth didn't happen overnight. Over five months they missed only about 10 days and went live roughly 1,500 hours. Stay consistent and you'll build market share, returning buyers and a community.

knowledge.question: Does Whatnot give new sellers a boost?
knowledge.answer: Levi believes there's a beginner boost for your first few streams; he had 80–90 viewers his first three days and has seen it with every streamer he's worked with. He says if you go in prepared and with energy, you'll get that boost.

knowledge.question: What's the best time and day to go live on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says Mondays are his best days. For time, he likes late night around 11 p.m. to midnight because competitors are asleep and people are lying in bed swiping, so there's less competition. His rule: go live when no one else wants to go live. Also remember buyers in other time zones like California, Hawaii and US territories are still awake.

knowledge.question: Is now a good time to start on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi says there's no better time than today. From what he's seen in his and other categories, streamers are down about 50% from the summer because side hustlers went back to their jobs, while viewers are up and the app keeps growing. That means less competition and supply with rising demand.

knowledge.question: How long should my live shows be?
knowledge.answer: Levi's electronics shows run about six to eight hours depending on the day, and hosts know to expect that. On a good day they push longer because tomorrow could be slow. If it's dead after four hours, the host's energy drops too, since they feed off the chat.

knowledge.question: What Whatnot fees should I expect?
knowledge.answer: Levi says it's 5% for electronics and coins, 8% for everything else, plus a 2.9% processing fee and 30 cents per transaction. Bundles help because the 30-cent transaction fee is charged once for the bundle instead of on every individual item.

knowledge.question: Why does bundling multiple items per box increase profit?
knowledge.answer: Levi says bundles make you more money because labor cost per unit decreases, shipping speeds up, and sell-through rate goes through the roof. Packing about 10 items per box means fewer boxes to ship for the same number of units, and his team passes savings on by filling boxes beyond the usual five-item bundle.

knowledge.question: Why is shipping so important on Whatnot?
knowledge.answer: Levi calls shipping the number one thing to focus on, because that's why people shop on Whatnot. If you only offer a three-item bundle and someone else offers 10, buyers, especially far away ones, will shop with the other seller. Your shipping has to make sense for the buyer; a $10 product with $9 shipping doesn't. He sets his shipping so 95–98% of orders land in Priority Mail.

knowledge.question: Are shipping supplies expensive when starting out?
knowledge.answer: No, Levi says shipping supplies are the cheapest thing on Whatnot. One weekend they sold $25,000 in two days and spent only about $50 on supplies. USPS Priority Mail boxes are free (make an account on USPS.com), they reuse brown boxes from incoming inventory, and poly bags are 30–40 cents each, so you mainly pay for tape and poly bags.

knowledge.question: Who pays shipping on heavy items, and how does it affect bids?
knowledge.answer: The buyer pays shipping, and each buyer sees a different price based on distance. Levi's example: a heavy $100 product with $25 shipping to California means that buyer may only bid $25, while a New Jersey buyer with $15 shipping might bid $10 more, and that extra goes to you. Box pricing is based on cubic inches (12x12x12 is about 1,728), so a long, thin item like a keyboard can still fit the range.

knowledge.question: How should I structure my shipping team?
knowledge.answer: Levi has one full-time main shipper plus on-demand helpers she can call in whenever needed, without even asking him. He likes to hire part-time, slowly build people up, and bring them on full-time once he really needs them. Shippers only pack; they don't stream.

knowledge.question: When should I hire a host?
knowledge.answer: Levi decided in his very first week. After doing $8,000 in revenue his first Friday through Sunday with a part-time helper, he ran virtual interviews on Indeed and had a team show up within days. He notes he already had the capital to do that.

knowledge.question: Do I have to be the host forever?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi says people think they have to host for the rest of their lives, but your hosts can build a community around themselves. If you're hosting 12 hours a day, you can't improve the business because your time goes into what he sees as lower-ROI work. Become the business owner, not the business.

knowledge.question: What does the business owner actually do once hosts and a manager are in place?
knowledge.answer: Levi's job now is mainly buying inventory. When he shows up, his job is to make everything more efficient, find better deals and talk to people. He says that's what separates six figures from seven figures.

knowledge.question: Should I use virtual assistants for my Whatnot business?
knowledge.answer: Yes. Levi says if a virtual assistant can do it, he'll hire one, rather than paying full US income for tasks like listing products. He uses overseas VAs for listing and bookkeeping and is building SOPs to train more. You can outsource almost anything; you just have to train them.

knowledge.question: How should I handle bookkeeping?
knowledge.answer: Levi tracks everything he buys to the penny and tracks average cost of goods. His virtual assistant handles it for him and is more organized than he is.

knowledge.question: Should I rent a warehouse or keep using storage units?
knowledge.answer: Levi says don't rush into a three-year lease; people make mistakes rushing and end up losing money. Storage units let you scale quickly month-to-month; if you need more space, get another unit and drop it when inventory sells through. When choosing a warehouse, he values being close to home and having a reasonable landlord, even over a cheaper place 45 minutes away.

knowledge.question: Should I store a lot of inventory?
knowledge.answer: No. Levi says you're not in the business of holding inventory; the goal is to process more inventory at a higher scale. With 36 pallets in, his team blew through about 15 in four or five days because he knew more deals were coming, and once he's made his money back the rest is profit.

knowledge.question: How can I start on Whatnot with under $100?
knowledge.answer: Levi says buy a storage unit for about $50 on sites like StorageTreasures.com or StorageAuctions.com, looking through photos for at least 500 items. Sell 500 items at $1 each and you've 10x'd your money. He made six figures flipping storage units before Whatnot existed.

knowledge.question: How do I get consistent inventory and the best deals?
knowledge.answer: Talk to people. Levi says you have to call, text and meet suppliers; that's how you get the best deals and consistent inventory, and eventually they'll call you. He started with a liquidator and then went straight to the source, skipping brokers. For closeouts, go to trade shows like ASD.
